nodes.label: Three-Layer Key Architecture
nodes.rationale: Only Layer 1 (KeyGenerator) is user-controlled; Layers 2 (UUID hashing) and 3 (store keying) are automatic, so application code never has to think about column widths or namespacing.

nodes.label: DefaultKeyGenerator
nodes.rationale: Args are converted to a raw string joined by ':'. Types with an identity toString() fall back to ClassName@hexHashCode, which is unstable across restarts, so a WARN is logged once per type (once, to avoid flooding the hot path).

nodes.label: FailoverKeyGenerator (UUID hashing, Layer 2)
nodes.rationale: UUID.nameUUIDFromBytes(effectiveName + ':' + rawKey) yields a fixed 36-char key: it prevents VARCHAR(256) overflow in the JDBC store, obscures business data at rest, and is deterministic so the same inputs always resolve the same entry.

nodes.label: FailoverNameResolver / effectiveName
nodes.rationale: effectiveName = domain.isBlank() ? name : domain. Two annotations sharing a domain hash with the same namespace prefix and store under the same FAILOVER_NAME, enabling cross-failover sharing. Logging still uses name (not effectiveName) so log lines stay distinguishable within a domain.

nodes.label: Key Stability Requirement
nodes.rationale: The same args must produce the same key at store and recover time, on every instance and across restarts. Pitfalls: identity toString/hashCode, unordered collections (Set iteration order), non-deterministic components (timestamps, request ids), and collisions from incomplete business identifiers.

nodes.label: Custom KeyGenerator bean
nodes.rationale: A custom generator completely replaces DefaultKeyGenerator — there is no partial delegation — so normalisation (sorting CSV, uppercasing) must be done wholly inside it.

edges.source_location: preventing VARCHAR(256) overflow in the JDBC store
